source.journal_name: Romanian Journal of Information Science and Technology

paper.title: An implementation of the backtracking algorithm for multicore systems
paper.abstract: The emergence of inexpensive parallel computers powered by multicore chips combined with high clock rates raises new challenges for software engineering. Since the performance improvements will not come from increased clock rates, high performance applications will need to be parallelized. In addition to operating system support, adjustments to existing software are required to maximize utilization of the computing resources provided by multicore processors. The ability of multicore processors to increase application performance depends on the use of multiple threads within applications. We will describe an algorithm that allows backtracking problems to be solved by means of such multicore systems. A multicore algorithm meant for backtracking problems and able to meet certain constraints is made of multiple search threads with concurrent operation and distinct processing parts of the solution space. The proposed algorithm is scalable.

artifact_assessment.evidence: no availability statement or link in the text; the implementation is mentioned only as "The multicore backtracking algorithm is implemented using C and Pthreads[18][19]."

flag_details.FORMALISM_THEATER: Level 2 paper (a fixed-depth split of textbook backtracking across threads, timed on n-queens) with 14 of 19 formal elements failing the Necessity Test (Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no). The configuration notation, its initial, solution and terminal configurations, the four transition rules, and the main- and secondary-thread configurations each restate the prose sentence before them and a branch of the pseudocode, and no proof or bound is derived from them; termination is asserted in prose, not proved.
flag_details.UNNECESSARY_SET_THEORY: The used-out values Ck ⊂ Vk are handled with set algebra in all three pseudocode listings and in the transition rules (Ci = ϕ for all i, Ck ≠ Vk, choose vk from Vk − Ck, Ck = Ck ∪ {vk}), yet with Vk = {1, ..., sk} the paper replaces each Ck by the integer vk: the union is an increment, the difference is the values above the counter, the empty set is zero. No proof depends on these operations.

verdict.summary: Fixed-depth split of textbook backtracking across Pthreads threads, timed on n-queens (n = 15-18) on up to four cores: a Level 2 contribution dressed in set algebra and configuration matrices that restate the prose and pseudocode, with sets the paper itself replaces by integer counters. One relevant self-citation; narrow evaluation; no code or data released.

papers.provenance:
## Formalism Analysis

### Concept Complexity
**Topic:** Running the textbook backtracking search on a shared-memory multicore machine. A main thread enumerates the consistent assignments of the first t components of the solution vector and starts a Pthreads thread for each; every secondary thread runs ordinary backtracking on components t+1 to n and passes its solutions back. The method is timed on the n-queens problem (n = 15 to 18, several values of t) on up to four cores (a dual AMD Opteron 280 system and an AMD Opteron 1218 system).
**Level:** 2 (Low)
**Rationale:** The contribution is a static split of the search tree at a fixed depth t, a simple modification of an existing method, followed by a timing study. There is no complexity or speedup analysis and no proof. Section 2, roughly five of the fourteen pages, re-presents the standard sequential algorithm. Level 3 would need a genuinely novel algorithm with analysis; the paper offers neither.

### Formal Elements
- Definitions: 4, all inline, none numbered (with constraints: 1, the solution vector): the solution vector x = (x1, ..., xn) with xi ∈ Vi; the space of possible solutions V1 × ... × Vn; Ck, the set of values used out for xk, with Ck ⊂ Vk; the two-row configuration notation
- Theorems: 0
- Proofs: 0
- Equations: 14 (f(n) = a^n; 2^n; Vk = {1, ..., sk}; the initial, solution and terminal configurations; four transition rules; two main-thread transitions; the secondary-thread terminal configuration; the efficiency ratio), plus the set operations inside the three pseudocode listings

The three pseudocode listings are the algorithm itself and are not tested as formalism; the set notation inside them is.

### Necessity Test
- Solution vector x = (x1, ..., xn), xi ∈ Vi, satisfying the constraints: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary (fixes what the code computes and introduces the index k on which both loops and the threshold t operate)
- Space of possible solutions V1 × V2 × ... × Vn: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary (a naming sentence; no size or bound is derived from the product, and the later remarks on subspaces are in prose)
- f(n) = a^n, a > 1, with the estimate for a = 3, n = 50: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 yes → necessary (carries the order-of-magnitude cost argument)
- 2^n subsets of an n-element set: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 yes → necessary (the output size bounds the work from below)
- Ck, the set of used-out values, Ck ⊂ Vk: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary (the paper itself replaces it by the integer vk)
- Set operations in the three pseudocode listings (Ci = ϕ ∀i, Ck ≠ Vk, choose vk from Vk − Ck, Ck = Ck ∪ {vk}, Ck = ϕ): Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary (as implemented they are a comparison of a counter with sk, the next integer, an increment, and a reset to zero)
- Domain simplification Vk = {1, 2, ..., sk}, with Ck represented by vk: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary (the representation decision that turns the sets into integer counters)
- Configuration notation (the values assigned, written over the used-out sets): Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary
- Initial configuration (x1 ... xn over ϕ ... ϕ): Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary
- Solution configuration (v1 ... vn over C1 ... Cn), from which the test k = n + 1 is read: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary (the test is already in the pseudocode)
- Rule 1, assign a value and advance: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary
- Rule 2, attempt failed: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary
- Rule 3, backtracking after a failed attempt: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary
- Rule 4, backtracking after a solution: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary
- Terminal configuration (x1 ... xn over V1 ϕ ... ϕ), from which the stop at k = 0 is read: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary (the guard k > 0 is already in the pseudocode, and termination is asserted rather than proved)
- Main-thread transition at k = t, handing the prefix to a new thread: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary
- Main-thread transition backtracking after the hand-off, with Ct ∪ {vt}: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary
- Secondary-thread terminal configuration (with Vt+1 used out), from which the stop at k = t is read: Q1 yes, Q2 no, Q3 no → unnecessary (the guard k > t is already in the listing)
- Efficiency, time for one core / (c × time for c cores), in percent: Q1 yes, Q2 yes, Q3 no → necessary (defines the reported quantity)

Each transition display is preceded by a sentence that states the same change of state in prose, and each corresponds to one branch of a pseudocode listing, so the displays state nothing the prose cannot (Q1) and constrain nothing the listings do not already fix (Q2). The nearest the notation comes to carrying an argument is the termination remark that no configuration can be reached twice; it is a one-sentence assertion in prose, and no proof is built on the displays (Q3).

### Proportionality
Calculated complexity: 8 (4 inline definitions × 2; no theorems, no proofs)
Expected range (Level 2): 0-15
Ratio: 0.53x upper bound

**Assessment:** Proportionate by count. The problem is necessity, not volume: 14 of the 19 tested elements perform none of the three functions. There are no Definition blocks, so `DECORATIVE_DEFINITIONS` is not raised; the inline namings are judged by the Necessity Test above.

### Issues
After writing the general algorithm in set algebra, the paper observes that with Vk = {1, ..., sk} and values tried in ascending order each Ck is {1, ..., vk}, and that this lets the author "replace the sets in the algorithm by numbers". The unions, differences and empty sets of the three listings are therefore increments, the values above a counter, and zero. The two-row configuration matrices, about a dozen displays over pp. 245-249, re-express the same four branches of the loop once more. The paper can be followed completely from its prose and pseudocode.

---

## Citation Analysis

One self-citation in 19 references (SCR 5.3%): [16], the author's 2008 paper on a distributed version of the same backtracking algorithm, cited as its distributed counterpart and therefore directly relevant (similarity about 0.9). The authors cited more than once are those of the distributed algorithms and comparisons the introduction describes ([3]-[12]); nothing suggests a citation ring. The list is relevant but thin on the paper's own setting: ten references cover distributed, agent-based constraint satisfaction ([3]-[12]), which the paper contrasts with its approach without comparing against any of it experimentally; three concern multicore parallelism ([13]-[15]); five are vendor pages, a standard, or a tutorial ([1], [2], [17]-[19]). Section 2's presentation of the sequential algorithm and its configuration notation carries no citation. No issues of citation conduct.

---

## Structural Analysis

The central claim, that the algorithm scales, rests on timing figures for n-queens with n = 15 to 18 on up to four cores. The prose reports that doubling the cores roughly halves the time and that n = 18 falls from over 32 hours to about 8 hours on four cores. The figures are images and their values are absent from the text extraction, so the assessment relies on the prose that reports them. Only one problem is tested; no run is repeated or given a spread; the paper does not say whether the one-core time in the efficiency ratio is that of the sequential program or of the threaded one, nor how the secondary threads, one per consistent prefix, are scheduled onto the cores. The explanations offered for the effect of t (thread creation and communication cost for t > 2 at n ≤ 16, more uniform threads at n > 16) are not measured. Three claims have no evidence: that the method controls message counts much better than agent-based approaches (no message counts are measured for either), that agent approaches need thousands of messages for n = 8 (no source), and that a failed core is recovered by restarting one secondary thread (neither implemented nor tested). The text refers Figure 2 to a third example, though the paper has only Example 1.

CER is about 0.6 (some 30-35 evidence-bearing sentences, mostly the cited statements of the introduction and the reported timings, against about 55 claim sentences): adequate. Limitations are acknowledged inline: the conclusion concedes low efficiency for small jobs, attributed to communication and thread-creation cost, and Section 3 notes the longer total time for t > 2 at n ≤ 16. There is no limitations section.

Artifacts: no code, data, or availability statement (see the evidence field). The benchmark needs no dataset, but the C/Pthreads program and its timings are what a reader would need to check the speedups, and neither is released (category `none`, relevant).

---

## Conclusion

The paper parallelises backtracking in the simplest way, by cutting the search tree at depth t and giving each subtree to a thread, and reports near-linear speedup for large n-queens instances on up to four cores. That is a modest Level 2 contribution. Its formal apparatus is not modest: the general algorithm is written in set algebra that the paper itself then reduces to integer counters, and every branch of the loop is restated as a two-row configuration matrix that adds nothing to the sentence before it or to the pseudocode, and from which no proof is drawn. Under the zero-tolerance rule for Level 1-2 papers this is formalism theater and unnecessary set theory, both disqualifying.

Citation conduct is clean, with one relevant self-citation. The evidence is narrow (one benchmark, no variance, results only in figures), the comparative and fault-tolerance claims are untested, and nothing is released.
